processing_steps.processing_steps_notes: Ingots homogenized at 1200 °C for 24 h before hot rolling.
Hot-rolled into plates with a thickness of 4 mm.
Solution treated at 1100 °C for 10 min under an argon atmosphere, followed by oil quenching. This is the parent process (proc_st-1100c-10min-oq) for the 600 °C/1 h aging.
Aging treatment defining this sample: solution-treated 15Al alloy aged at 600 °C for 1 h, followed by water quenching. Reported hardness for this condition = 904.9 ± 30.2 HV (Table 2).

structures.overall_structure: After aging the 15Al alloy at 600 °C for 1 h, the α (BCC) matrix had almost completely transformed into β-Mn within just 1 h, and abundant fine precipitates (identified as BCC and FCC phases) were present within the β-Mn. SE-SEM of the 600 °C/1 h condition shows a smooth, uniform β-Mn matrix.

phases_present.morphology: dominant matrix; smooth uniform β-Mn matrix in SE-SEM
fine precipitates within/at interfaces of β-Mn

precipitates.distribution: within the β-Mn / between β-Mn interfaces

interfaces.phase_evolution: α → α + FCC Cu-rich phase → α-Mn + β-Mn + BCC phase → β-Mn + BCC phase + FCC Cu-rich phase
interfaces.interface_notes: The interface phases (BCC and FCC Cu-rich) form between the β-Mn grains because β-Mn is a Mn-rich phase whose nucleation/growth expels Fe, Al and Cu into the surrounding matrix; Al enrichment stabilizes the BCC phase and limited Cu solubility produces the FCC Cu-rich phase. Note: the interface microstructures were characterized in detail by TEM only on the hardest 15Al sample (600 °C/6 h), not on the present 600 °C/1 h sample.

measurement_conditions.other_conditions: Vickers microhardness measured on an HVS-1000 tester with a load of 9.8 N for 15 s; each sample tested 5 times and the average reported. Sample aged at 600 °C for 1 h.

characterization_methods.measurement_conditions: Load 9.8 N for 15 s; each sample tested 5 times, average reported; electrolytically polished samples (10% perchloric acid + 90% ethanol)
characterization_methods.purpose: Measure Vickers hardness of the 15Al alloy after aging treatments
characterization_methods.key_findings: 15Al alloy aged at 600 °C for 1 h reached 904.9 ± 30.2 HV (Table 2); at temperatures of 575 °C and above the aging hardening response was significantly accelerated, with a substantial hardness increase after just 1 h of aging.

characterization_methods.instrument_or_setup: ZEISS Sigma 300 SEM operated at 5 kV
characterization_methods.measurement_conditions: Electrolytically polished samples (10% perchloric acid + 90% ethanol); 50 μm scale bar main fields, 10 μm insets
characterization_methods.purpose: Identify the precipitation of secondary phases (α-Mn and β-Mn) in the aged 15Al alloy
characterization_methods.key_findings: The 600 °C/1 h panel of Fig. 7 shows a smooth, uniform matrix carrying a green β-Mn label, consistent with the near-complete α→β-Mn transformation in 1 h at 600 °C.

unmapped_findings: Alloy 15Al (Fe-35Mn-15Al-5Cu at.%) EDS chemical composition (Table 1): Fe 44.6, Mn 35.2, Al 15.0, Cu 5.2 at.%; nominal Fe-35Mn-15Al-5Cu (at.%).

The 15Al alloy density is 6.85 g/cm³ (Archimedes method); the alloy achieved an ultra-high specific hardness of 141 HV·cm³/g at its peak-hardness condition (600 °C/6 h, 965.6 HV), not at the present 600 °C/1 h condition.

Fracture toughness KIC of the hardest 15Al sample (600 °C/6 h, 965.6 HV) is 8.6 MPa·m^1/2 (average crack length 18 μm); KIC was measured only on peak-hardness samples, so it is not a value of the 600 °C/1 h sample.

β-Mn intrinsic hardness in the hardest 15Al sample = 12.1 ± 0.3 GPa (nanoindentation); β-Mn composition in the hardest 15Al sample = Mn 36.8, Al 14.3, Cu 2.8 at.% (SEM-EDS). These refer to the peak-hardness (600 °C/6 h) sample, not the 600 °C/1 h sample.
The solution-treated 15Al baseline Vickers hardness is 253.4 ± 2.1 HV (Table 2).
